title: Insights into the role of retained austenite stability in TRIP-aided steel: Ductilizing and toughening
abstract: This study investigates the tensile and impact property of TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity)-aided steel with different retained austenite (RA) stability at different temperatures. The RA stability of experimental steels processed by hot rolling-coiling at 450 °C, short tempering and long duration tempering followed the sequence: un-temper (C450) < short (C450-ST) < long duration tempering (C450-LT). With the tempering time increases, the stability of RA gradually improves. The improvement of RA stability with different degrees resulted in significant improvements in ductility and toughness, respectively. These findings emphasize that maintaining uniform distribution of stable RA during different stages of tensile straining promotes continuous TRIP effect, resulting in an increased level of strain hardening and enhanced ductility. However, RA with higher stability experienced plastic deformation followed by TRIP effect during impact deformation, which effectively blunts the crack tips thereby inhibiting brittle fracture and leading to higher impact toughness. RA stability had a dual and important effect on ductility and toughness. Continuous and gradual TRIP effect enhanced ductility, while extensive and short-lived TRIP effect was detrimental to toughness.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: There is significant interest to employ advanced high strength steels (AHSS) to reduce the weight of automobile structure. Many applications requiring good formability and high structural properties require high strength, ductility and toughness. However, these properties are mutually exclusive, that is, the strength-ductility/toughness tradeoff. The transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect plays a key role in the tradeoff between strength and ductility/toughness during deformation [ 1–7 ]. The stability of retained austenite is the key to TRIP effect [ 8–11 ].

Previous studies have shown that the TRIP effect during tensile tests is beneficial. Retained austenite transformed to martensite during deformation inhibited necking [ 12 ]. A higher volume fraction of austenite correlates with better uniform elongation in steel [ 13 ]. However, high ductility in AHSSs does not mean that a high toughness is ensured. Previous studies have shown that there is no direct correlation between impact toughness and ductility. The effect of RA on impact toughness is contradictory. On the one hand, the general consensus is that the TRIP effect has the potential to enhance toughness, because TRIP effect can promote plastic deformation [ 14 , 15 ]. When the crack propagation encountered metastable austenite, the crack tip is passivated. The high stress generated by the crack tip renders metastable austenite to transform to martensite, absorbing energy and preventing crack propagation [ 16–18 ]. The positive impacts of TRIP-toughening or TRIP-induced crack termination mechanism are frequently cited to account for the outstanding fatigue and fracture characteristics of steels [ 19–21 ]. However, brittle martensite formation increases the odds of brittle crack propagation [ 16 , 22–24 ].

Heterogeneous structure design has proved to be an effective method to solve the balance between material strength and ductility/toughness [ 25–32 ]. The dual phase microstructure of bainite/martensite (B/M) offers an advantage compared to the conventional single-phase martensite or bainite structure, as it combines strength and toughness [ 33–35 ]. With similar austenite grain size, the toughness of steel can be enhanced by the B/M microstructure due to its ability to hinder crack propagation through finer packet sizes [ 36–40 ]. TRIP-aided steel is a AHSS with the above-mentioned B/M heterogeneous structure. It has good strength-plastic and toughness, in which carbon-rich retained austenite is the key factor influencing TRIP effect [ 41 , 42 ]. In previous studies, the austenite volume fraction of most control group samples varied greatly, and the process, microstructure, or composition were different [ 43–45 ]. However, a comprehensive investigation into the individual effect of austenite stability on the ductility and toughness of TRIP-aided steel remains to be fully understood.

In this study, we maintained a consistent control of the austenite content. Our research ensures the reduction of the impact of matrix microstructure differences on ductility and toughness, in order to investigate the individual effect of austenite stability on ductility and toughness. We designed a TRIP-aided steel with different austenite stability by tailoring the heat treatment. Our study explains how the stability of RA has a dual effect on the ductility and toughness of TRIP-aided steel. The new knowledge derived from the present study provides valuable insights which will enable the development of futuristic steel designs with different combinations of strength, ductility, and toughness.

sections.heading: Experimental
paragraphs: An experimental steel of composition Fe-0.18C-2.05Mn-1.85(Si + Al)-0.025Nb (wt.%) was melted in a vacuum and cast into a steel ingot of ∼80 mm thick. Next, it was homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h and hot rolled to ∼12 mm thick strip after several passes, and the minimum reduction rate of each pass was ∼25%.

JMatPro (Version 11.0) was used to calculate the bainite start temperature (Bs) which was 500 °C and the martensite starting temperature (Ms) which was 364 °C [ 46 ].  Fig. 1 
                       shows heat treatment processes. After austenitizing for 30 min in air furnace at 960 °C and cooling in an air furnace at 450 °C, this condition is referred as C450. Anisothermal bainite transformation involves a gradual reduction in temperature. Carbon partitioned from bainite to untransformed austenite [ 47 , 48 ]. When the temperature is lower than the Ms point of untransformed austenite, martensitic transformation occurs. The C450 steel was subjected to tempering at 300 °C for 0.5 h and 12 h, followed by air cooling to room temperature, resulting in the designation of C450-ST and C450-LT, respectively.

We used a Z100 TEW tester at room temperature at a strain rate of 10 −3  S −1  for tensile tests. The dimensions of the tensile sample were 50 mm in length, 10 mm in width, and 1.5 mm in thickness, with the load applied parallel to the direction of rolling of the plate. The samples for tensile testing were prepared in accordance with the ASTM-E8 standard. CVN impact test was carried out on samples with dimensions of 10 mm × 5 mm × 55 mm using 450 J instrument pendulum impact testing machine. The impact sample's v-shaped notch was aligned with the transverse steel plate. The ductile-brittle transition temperature (DBTT) curve of the steels was measured within the range of −40 °C–300 °C. Three impact tests were executed for each condition to gain an average toughness.

The microstructure of steel was analyzed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with JSM-6700F FE-SEM, electron back scatter diffraction (EBSD) with Oxford EBSD detector, transmission electron microscopy (TEM) with JEM-F200, X-ray diffraction (XRD) with 3 KW D/MAX2200V PC and three-dimensional atomic probe tomography (3D-APT) with LEAP 4000 X HR. The EBSD data was processed using the Oxford-HKL Channel 5 software. Samples for SEM, EBSD, and XRD analysis underwent grinding and mechanical polishing following standard metallographic protocols. The samples were etched with 4% nitrate alcohol solution and electrolytically polished with a solution of ethanol with 10% perchloric acid. TEM samples were prepared by electropolishing with 10% perchloric acid in ethanol at −20 °C using 3 mm diameter specimens. The needle-shaped samples analyzed by 3D-APT were prepared by electrolytic polishing. The atomic probe data were reconstructed and analyzed with the use of IVASTM 3.6.2 software.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties
paragraphs:
The engineering stress-strain plot of experimental steels is shown in  Fig. 2 
                         a. The mechanical properties of the three experimental steels are presented in  Table 1 
                         . The yield strength (YS) and tensile strength (UTS) of tempered steels are significantly lower than coiled steels. The total elongation of C450 steel was ∼15%. The ductility of the coiled and tempered steels was superior than the coiled steel, and the total elongation of C450-LT steel was about 7% lower than C450-ST steel.

The impact toughness of experimental steel in terms of ductile-brittle transition temperature DBTT curve is shown in  Fig. 2 b. High temperature impact samples are heated using a small-sized air furnace. The sample was kept in air furnace for 8 min. It can avoid affecting the microstructure while ensuring that the sample has been heated to target temperature. Low-temperature impact specimens prepared by immersing experimental steel in alcohol cooled by liquid nitrogen for 8 min to the target temperature. The CVN absorption energy of samples for the upper shelf is essentially similar. C450, C450-ST and C450-LT steels all showed typical ductile-brittle transition with the decrease of test temperature. At identical temperature, C450-LT steel showed higher CVN energy than C450-ST and C450T steels, and the toughness was increased after tempering. DBTT is defined as the temperature corresponding to half of the sum of the energy of the upper and lower shelves. The DBTTs of three steels were 125 °C, 90 °C and 30 °C, respectively. The DBTTs of the experimental steels decreased significantly with the increase of tempering time.

sections.heading: Microstructural characterization
paragraphs:
Fig. 3 
                          displays the SEM image of the experimental steels. The microstructure of C450 steel ( Fig. 3 a) consisted of typical lath bainite (B), dispersed M/A islands, and filmy RA. The microstructure of C450-ST steel ( Fig. 3 b) had no significant change compared with the C450 steel. When the tempering time was extended to 12 h, some M/A islands in C450-LT steel showed obvious decomposition ( Fig. 3 c). Bainite transformation occurred in some of large blocky RA ( Fig. 3 c). All steels have a minor presence of ferrite (F).

The phase distribution, grain boundary (GB) and inverse pole figure (IPF) of EBSD results are presented in  Fig. 4 
                         . The austenite volume fractions observed by EBSD were 7.2%, 6.8% and 4.9%, respectively. This value will be lower than the results measured by XRD. This is because the resolution of EBSD is limited, and some small-sized RAs such as filmy RA cannot be observed. The volume fraction of RA gradually decreases with tempering time ( Fig. 4 a–c, e). Large size blocky RA is mainly distributed along the prior austenite grain boundaries. Compared with C450 and C450-ST steels, the volume fraction of large size blocky RA is significantly reduced in C450-LT steel. Film-like RA interpenetrates between martensitic laths. The density of high angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) of C450, C450-ST and C450-LT are 1.69 ,1.72, 1.68 μm −1 , respectively. No significant difference in HAGBs was observed in tempered steels ( Fig. 4 a–c, e), which indicated that there was no momentous effect on microstructure refinement with the tempering time prolonged.

Fig. 5 
                          shows the area-weighted fraction distribution of FCC grain size of steels by using EBSD statistics. After tempering 0.5 h, RA above 6 μm 2  significantly decreased, the RA distribution of 4–5 μm 2  in C450 steel gradually shifts to 3–4 μm 2 . After tempering 12 h, RA above 4 μm 2  gradually disappeared, and the distribution of the smallest RA size further decreased.

Fig. 6 
                          displays a TEM image of the experimental steel along with the associated selection area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern. The microstructure of C450 steel is composed of lath bainite, filmy RA between the lath and M/A island ( Fig. 6 a and b). After tempering, the matrix structure of the steels continued to dominate by lath bainite and inter lath filmy RA ( Fig. 6 c, d, e, f). Some of the block RA was decomposed on tempering. In summary, with the tempering time prolonged, the matrix microstructure had no change. All of them were composed of lath bainite, M/A island and film-like RA between the lath bainite.  Fig. 7 
                          shows the observations in STEM mode, where the change of dislocation density in the microstructure can be observed. With the tempering time prolonged, the dislocation density gradually decreased.

Fig. 8 
                         a shows XRD analysis results. The volume fraction of RA calculated by using the method mentioned in section  2  is listed in  Table 2

Due to the EBSD results mainly observing large size blocky RA, so the volume fraction of the filmy RA in three steels is about the difference value of the XRD results and the EBSD results. The estimated volume fractions of filmy RA in C450, C450-ST and C450-LT are as follows: 9.8%, 7.2% and 6.1%. Due to some filmy RA can still be detected by EBSD, these values may be slightly lower than the actual values.

sections.heading: Effect of tempering on the stability of austenite
paragraphs: It is widely recognized that the stability of RA is affected by carbon content [ 55 ], C partitioning between different interfaces [ 56 , 57 ], morphology [ 58 , 59 ], dislocation density [ 60 ], grain size [ 61 , 62 ]. This section offers an in-depth discussion of the factors that impact the stability of RA.

                         γ  is the volume fraction of austenite at true strain  ε , and  k  is defined to be the stability coefficient of RA. The  k  reflects the mechanical stability of RA. The higher the value of  k , the lower the mechanical stability of RA, and the faster is the transformation of retained austenite to martensite. In this study, the  k  values of C450, C450-ST and C450-LT steels are calculated by equation  (2)  are 16.53, 6.62 and 4.13, respectively, which indicated that the RA in C450-LT steel shows higher stability than the other two steels. C450 steel exhibits intensive and short-lived TRIP effect, while C450-ST steel exhibits a continuous and gradual TRIP effect. C450-LT does not undergo notable TRIP effect due to the high stability of RA.

Previous experiments and TEM results confirmed that the carbon present in martensite did not undergo consumption of the formation of carbides while tempering, but was partitioned to austenite [ 46 ]. Due to the high carbon content, the diffraction peaks of austenite generally shift to the left [ 64 ]. Compared with C450 steel, the peak position of (200)γ austenite in C450-ST and C450-LT steels shifted to the left ( Fig. 10 
                         ), indicating further enrichment of austenite stabilizing elements in RA during tempering [ 64 ]. According to calculation of  formula 1 , the carbon content of RA in the C450, C450-ST and C450-LT steels were 0.59 wt.%, 0.8 wt.% and 0.95 wt.%, respectively. With the increase of tempering time gradually extended to 12 h, carbon content of RA increased from 0.59 wt.% to 0.95 wt.%. On extending tempering time, the enriched carbon in retained austenite was higher, as implied by the XRD results.

Fig. 11 
                          shows the atomic probe tomography (APT) carbon isoconcentration surface analysis of the experimental steels.  Table 3 
                          shows the one-dimensional concentration analysis results which carbon content of austenite in steels. Due to the uneven distribution of carbon, the carbon content of individual RA may be higher than the average value measured by XRD. The austenite of C450 is insufficient stable at room temperature. The carbon content of austenite gradually increases with tempering time prolonged indicates that carbon is further partitioned into austenite during the tempering process, thus enhancing the stability of austenite [ 13 ]. The trend is consistent with the XRD results and indicates that the degree of carbon enrichment is higher in individual RA.

Furthermore, the average RA grain size of C450, C450-ST and C450-LT steels determined by EBSD was 2.1 μm 2 , 1.6 μm 2  and 1.3 μm 2 , respectively. The average grain size of RA decreased with the increase of tempering time. As indicated by XRD results, the volume fraction of austenite decreases with the increase of tempering time. We calculated the isothermal tempering process of the coiled steels using JMatPro, C450 can still occur bainite transformation from RA when isothermal tempering at 300 °C. The acicular bainite formed during isothermal tempering can divide the previous austenite, which facilitates the refinement of austenite grain size and improve its stability [ 65 ].

sections.heading: Effect of austenite stability on ductility
paragraphs:
Fig. 12 
                          shown the true work hardening rate (WHR) curve of the steels. The WHR curve of the steels divide into two different stages. The initial WHR value of C450 and C450-ST steels were both high which reaching approximately 5 GPa in 2.5% strain of Stage Ⅰ and decreased continuously from 3 GPa to 1 GPa before fracture in StageⅡ. The initial WHR value C450-LT is low which approximately 1.8 GPa, then decreased slowly, and the decrease rate is lower than C450 and C450-ST steels.

At low strain, C450 steel maintained a high strain hardening rate and experienced a strong TRIP effect, because RA in C450 steel is not very stable. C450-ST steel exhibited superior TRIP effect during tensile deformation and higher strain to fracture. The continuous TRIP effect alleviates the local stress concentration, delays the initiation of micro-cracks and occurrence of necking, and enhances the ductility [ 44 , 66 , 67 ]. However, RA stability of C450-LT steel is high, which hinders martensitic transformation during the tensile straining, and reduces ductility.

sections.heading: Effect of austenite stability on toughness
paragraphs:
The fracture surface of the experimental steels at room temperature shows a sharp contrast in  Fig. 13 
                         a–c. The overall surface of C450 steel is relatively flat. The surface roughness of C450-ST steel is greater than C450 steel. The fracture surface of C450-LT steel is more rugged ( Fig. 13 c).  Fig. 13 d–f shows enlarged view of the fracture surface. C450 steel is mainly cleavage surface ( Fig. 13 d). A few small dimples appeared on the surface of C450-ST steel fracture surface, but the fracture was mainly cleavage ( Fig. 13 e).  Fig. 13 f shows the fracture surface of C450-LT steel is characterized by a considerable quantity of dimples. More dimples were observed, which implies considerable plastic deformation of steel before fracture, contributing to high toughness [ 43 ].

Not only does the stability but also morphology and size of RA has effect on its toughness [ 68 ]. Previous studies improved toughness by reducing the volume fraction and size of blocky RA [ 24 , 69 ]. Large sized blocky RA is unstable and easily transforms into large-sized hard and brittle martensite during deformation, which has a crucial bad impact on toughness [ 23 ].

Compared with blocky RA, filmy RA can more effectively improve toughness by preventing crack propagation and assisting crack deflection [ 18 , 24 , 70 , 71 ]. In this study, although there was a slight reduction in the filmy RA, it is reported that such a reduction has a relatively small impact on toughness [ 18 , 72 , 73 ], while the improvement of filmy RA stability can significantly enhance toughness. Therefore, we will have a more in-depth discussion on the influence of RA stability on toughness.

It can be seen that RA with higher metastability corresponds to higher toughness at identical temperature and lower DBTT. This phenomenon is better explained by the temperature-dependent relationship curves between different stresses of each phase and yield stress plot ( Fig. 14

The austenite stability of C450 and C450-ST steels is lower. Due to stress concentration, RA rapidly transformed to martensite during the impact process at the crack tip [ 75 ]. This new martensite is transformed from carbon-rich RA, which is hard and brittle. The hard and brittle fresh martensitic grains unable to effectively adjust to the deformation of the surrounding matrix, which promotes the formation of secondary cracks [ 76 ]. The crack propagation path of the sample during the impact test at room temperature, as shown in  Fig. 15 
                         . At the interface between soft phase and hard phase, such as the interface between bainite matrix and martensite or M/A island, it is easily that voids/cracks will initiate and propagate [ 77 ] ( Fig. 15 a, b, c, d). Decohesion occurs between martensite and bainite matrix, causing fine brittle cracks to rapidly propagate along the M/A islands and the edges of the bainite matrix [ 22 ] ( Fig. 15 a and b). Thus, the crack of C450 and C450-ST steel propagated with brittle fine crack ( Fig. 15 b and c). The cause of this damage is associated with the disparity in hardness between newly formed martensite and bainite [ 78 ]. As a result, damage occurs and propagates in a brittle manner ( Fig. 13 ).

The more stable RA in C450-LT steel can delay the occurrence of TRIP, suppress brittle fracture, significantly passivate the crack tip, and thus provide superior impact toughness. The carbon in the matrix was partitioned to austenite, which reduces the difference of hardness between soft and hard phases. Given that it is not brittle and easy to deform, this result in reduced decohesion, which makes crack propagation through growth and coalescence of voids ( Fig. 15 e). Thus, the crack of C450-LT steel was ductile ( Fig. 15 f).

The martensite/bainite matrix dislocation recovery in C450-ST steel is limited. However, the longer tempering time of C450-LT steel causes more dislocation recovery in bainite/martensite ( Fig. 8 b), which improves its load bearing capacity during the strain process. Softening of the matrix through dislocation recovery can also improve toughness [ 79 ].

sections.heading: General discussion
paragraphs: To achieve a good synergy of strength, ductility and toughness of AHSS presents some challenges. It is commonly accepted that increased TRIP effect in steel contributes to improved ductility and toughness [ 14 , 15 ]. However, good ductility and toughness in the actual service conditions of AHSS requires different degree of RA stability.

During tensile straining, when RA stability is too low, TRIP effect is concentrated at low strain. When RA stability is too high, TRIP effect will not occur during the straining. Both the above situations lead to premature fracture of steel. Good ductility requires that the steel has RA with moderate stability and TRIP occurs continuously throughout the deformation process. On the contrary, low stability RA will prematurely undergo TRIP effect during the impact process, leading to hard and brittle transformed martensite. This process leads to rapid propagation of cracks along the boundaries of soft and hard phases. Previous studies mentioned that rapid martensite transformation rate reduces crack initiation energy [ 80 ]. The low stability of austenite leads to rapid martensite transformation rate. Compared with the tensile process, the triaxial stress during the impact process accelerates TRIP effect, which has rapid deformation-induced martensitic transformation (DIMT). These phenomena are not conducive to the toughness of the steels. Thus, under impact conditions, a more stable RA is needed to mitigate the TRIP effect.
The appropriate stability of RA can provide the desired TRIP effect in the AHSS design. Retained austenite stability has significant on ductility and toughness in a TRIP-aided steel.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
In this investigation, experimental steel with different austenite stability was obtained by controlling tempering time, and their tensile and fracture characteristics were evaluated and contrasted. According to the experimental results and discussion, the following conclusions can be drawn. 
                         
                            (1) 
                            Compared with C450 steel, the elongation of C450-ST steel significantly increased to 30%, while C450-LT steel decreased to 24%. with the increasingly tempering time. With the increase of tempering time, the RA stability was significantly enhanced, the DBTT first decreased slightly, and then significantly to 30 °C. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            During tensile straining, RA of C450-ST with different stability and volume fraction and uniform distribution in the matrix, TRIP gradually occurs during the entire straining process, which provides strain hardening behavior and improves the ductility of the material. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            During impact deformation, RA of C450 with low stability TRIP effect occurs prematurely to form hard and brittle fresh martensite, and the crack extension along with boundary of soft and hard phase propagates rapidly. However, RA of C450-LT with high stability first plastically deforms and passivates the crack tip and TRIP toughening occurs during the later stage of deformation and decreases DBTT. 
                         
                         
                            (4) 
                            Good ductility and toughness can be obtained steel with different RA stability. Continuous and gradual TRIP effect is conducive to the ductility of the steel, while the extensive and short-lived TRIP effect is not conducive to the toughness of steel.
